definition: A web tracking method using tiny, invisible images (1x1 pixels) embedded in emails, websites, or ads to collect information about user behavior and engagement.
metaDescription: Learn about pixel tracking - invisible images used to monitor user behavior, email opens, and website visits for analytics and advertising purposes.
simpleExplanation: Pixel tracking uses invisible tiny images to secretly monitor what you do online. When you open an email or visit a website, these hidden pixels automatically load and send information back to companies about your actions.
whyItMatters: Pixel tracking enables extensive surveillance of your online activities without your knowledge. It allows companies to build detailed profiles of your interests, track you across websites, and monitor personal behaviors like email reading habits.
technicalDetail: Tracking pixels are typically 1x1 pixel transparent GIF or PNG images with unique URLs. When loaded, they send HTTP requests containing user data like IP address, browser type, timestamp, and referrer information. Email pixels can detect opens, while web pixels enable cross-site tracking and conversion measurement.

examples.explanation: A retailer embeds a tracking pixel in their newsletter. When you open the email, the pixel loads and tells them you opened it, when you opened it, and what device you used.
An online store places pixels on product pages to track which items you view, how long you stay, and whether you make a purchase, helping them understand customer behavior.
Facebook places pixels on business websites to track your visits and purchases, then uses this data to show you targeted ads and measure ad effectiveness across platforms.
